payload.text: Walk me through how you'd approach this problem.

I would use a hash map. As I iterate through the array, for each element I check whether the complement, which is target minus the current value, has already been stored. If it has, I return the two indices. Otherwise I store the current value mapped to its index. That gives O of n time and O of n space.
Sounds reasonable. What's the worst-case complexity, and can you handle duplicates?

Worst case is O of n because we visit every element once and each hash map operation is O of one on average. Duplicates work because I check the map before inserting, so if target is twice the current value and we've already seen it, we get a valid pair.

code_rating.user_content:
## Interview Question
Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution; you may not use the same element twice.

## Brute Force Approach
Name: nested_loops
Complexity: {'time': 'O(n^2)', 'space': 'O(1)'}
Steps: ['For each i, for each j > i, check if nums[i]+nums[j]==target']

## Optimal Approach 1
Name: hash_map
Complexity: {'time': 'O(n)', 'space': 'O(n)'}
Steps: ['Iterate the array once', 'For each element, check if (target - element) is in the map', 'Otherwise store element -> index']

## Common Pitfalls
- Using the same index twice
- Returning values instead of indices

## Candidate's Code (language: python)
```python
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        complement = target - num
        if complement in seen:
            return [seen[complement], i]
        seen[num] = i
    return []

```
